Article Title: Tesla Bull Larry Goldberg wrote a long open letter to Bernie Sanders and everyone who say that Elon Musk is the face of everything wrong with billionaires, days later Spacex CEO responds
Article Text:
Elon Musk has a 'failure warning' for these technology companies; says: Investors have already started betting against them

Here's Larry Goldberg's open letter on Elon Musk

Popularly known as Tesla Bull, Larry Goldberg is an entrepreneur and investor. He is also co-author of the book 'The Decision Model'. Goldberg has started around 20 companies over the years, and sold his first software company at the dotcom peak in 1999. Early last month, Goldberg wrote a long open letter to everyone who he wrote say that Elon Musk is the face of everything wrong with billionaires.Days later, Elon Musk quoted his letter on X, and claimed how Tesla and Spacex have created wealth for their employees over the years. "Tesla and SpaceX have created meaningful wealth for hundreds of thousands of employees over time and improved the retirement savings of hundreds of millions of people," he wrote.Whenever Bernie Sanders and others on the left hold Elon up as the face of everything wrong with billionaires they omit some very pertinent facts: about 158,500 people draw a paycheck directly from one of Elon Musk's companies today, and by my estimate those companies will support roughly 870,000 jobs by the end of this year once you count the suppliers who make their parts and the local businesses where their workers spend their wages.By 2031, in my base case, that number climbs to about 1.4 million.Behind those figures are families making mortgage payments, putting kids through school and building careers in Austin, Brownsville, Fremont, Buffalo, Memphis and dozens, if not hundreds of other places in the US and around the world: they deserve a seat in the conversation.People will argue about wealth and taxes all day. My answer to the criticism is the arithmetic, so I went through the company filings and state records and counted the jobs as carefully as I could.Who works there todayThe direct count is about 158,500. Tesla reported 134,785 employees at the end of 2025 in its 10-K. SpaceX, which now includes xAI and X, reported more than 22,000 full-time employees at March 31 in its S-1 and has added roughly 350 more with Cursor since then. The Boring Company and Neuralink add about 1,350 between them, which is an estimate from LinkedIn-based trackers because neither company publishes headcount. I treat the total as a floor, since Tesla and SpaceX have both kept hiring since those filing dates.Looking out to the end of 2031, my base case reaches about 248,000 direct employees, with a low case near 171,000 and a high case around 377,000. Everything below the company level is my own estimate, built program by program to add up to the filed totals.Where the jobs areTexas is the center of gravity. Giga Texas had 16,506 workers in 2025 according to Travis County's compliance report, and Elon has said Tesla's Austin workforce will likely pass 30,000 by 2028. Starbase near Brownsville had about 4,200 SpaceX employees in March, local officials say the company plans to reach about 8,000 within 18 months, and Cameron County officials credit SpaceX with supporting more than 24,000 jobs in the area. Bastrop's Starlink factory had 1,590 workers in May, and there is a lot more coming behind it, including 3,000 jobs in the first phase of Terafab in Grimes County under the governor's announcement, 9,712 permanent jobs at full operation in the filing for Tesla's Fort Bend solar factory, 1,500 at the Brookshire Megafactory by 2028 and about 250 at the Robstown lithium refinery.The rest of the country has its own long list. Nevada's audited state reports show 7,283 Tesla employees at Gigafactory 1 at an average wage of $48.24 an hour, and the new Semi factory there just entered volume production. Fremont in California is reported at 20,000 to 22,000 workers, and Hawthorne builds Falcon rockets, Dragon capsules, Raptor engines and Starlink terminals. Tesla's Buffalo plant had 2,399 full-time workers at the end of 2025, with another 1,060 elsewhere in New York. In Memphis, xAI says it employs almost 3,000 people locally, a count that runs from electricians and engineers to cooks and construction workers, and Mississippi expects hundreds of permanent jobs from the more than $20 billion xAI is investing in Southaven. Florida's Starship deal carries at least 600 new jobs by 2030 on top of the hundreds SpaceX already employs at the Cape. Louisiana expects 3,000 direct jobs at Starbase Louisiana over ten years at an average salary of $92,600, and projects about 34,500 construction jobs at the peak of the build.The footprint reaches well beyond the US. Shanghai's last reported figure was about 20,000 workers in 2023, and Berlin is hiring back to about 12,700 people in vehicle production, with more than 1,500 further hires planned for its new battery cell plant.Where the growth comes fromRobotaxi operations are the single biggest addition in my base case, at roughly 16,750 people covering the depots, remote support and fleet care that a large autonomous fleet needs. Tesla's sales, service, engineering and corporate base adds about 11,300 as the fleet on the road roughly doubles, and Optimus adds about 10,600 if Fremont reaches a million robots a year. After that come vehicle manufacturing including Cybercab at about 6,700, battery cells at about 6,000, Fort Bend solar at about 5,800, Starbase Texas at about 4,900 and Terafab at about 2,900. Starbase Louisiana only reaches about 1,200 direct jobs by 2031, since construction starts next year and the first launch is 2029 at the earliest.To be fair about it, the low case is nearly flat, because Optimus and factory automation offset most of the new hiring. Even in the base case, productivity gains keep vehicle manufacturing far below the roughly 106,000 workers that kind of volume would otherwise take. I count that as a strength, because companies that keep getting more productive are the ones that can keep growing and keep paying well, and the next section shows why the wider job count keeps rising even when factory headcount doesn't.The wider footprintEvery one of these factories, launch sites and data centers buys parts, materials and services, and every paycheck gets spent at local businesses. Using the Economic Policy Institute's 2019 multipliers, which separate supplier jobs from jobs supported by worker spending, I estimate the companies' end-2026 workforce supports roughly 870,000 jobs in all once both layers are added to the direct staff. By 2031 that reaches about 0.93 million in the low case, 1.41 million in the base case and 2.27 million in the high case. Supplier jobs follow output, so a factory that makes more with fewer people keeps buying more parts and materials, which is why this total grows even in the low case. Worker-spending jobs follow headcount, since they come out of payroll.I'd hold these wider numbers more loosely than the direct ones, and the right way to describe them is jobs supported by Musk-company spending, since these suppliers also work for other customers. The multipliers are US national averages, so they overstate the effect of Shanghai and Berlin, where about half of Tesla's vehicle workforce sits. At US multipliers that group alone accounts for about 243,000 of the end-2026 supplier and spending jobs, and most of those would really be in China and Germany. The data center supplier figure is probably on the high side as well, and temporary construction work is a separate layer that isn't in any of these totals.The bottom lineElon's critics are entitled to their view of billionaires, but the numbers still matter. About 158,500 people work directly for his companies today, and if robotaxi, Optimus, chips and solar ramp roughly on plan, that could reach about 250,000 by 2031. Counting suppliers and worker spending, those companies will support roughly 870,000 jobs by the end of this year and about 1.4 million by 2031 in my base case, spread across Texas, Louisiana, Nevada, Florida, California, New York, Tennessee, Mississippi and factories around the world. That is a lot of American families, and plenty more beyond our borders, whose livelihoods are tied to what Elon builds.
Article Summary: Larry Goldberg is an entrepreneur and investor. He has started around 20 companies over the years, and sold his first software company at the dotcom peak in 1999. He wrote a long open letter to everyone who he wrote say that Elon Musk is the face of everything wrong with billionaires. His answer to the criticism is the arithmetic, so he counted the jobs as carefully as he could.

Article Title: Jeff Bezos commits $100 million to a $500 million wildlife alliance targeting 31,000 endangered species as global conservation funding falls short
Article Text:
Bezos Earth Fund backs $500 million alliance to protect endangered species

More than 31,000 species fall within the alliance’s target categories

Earlier Phoenix project targets 100 species across 30 countries

Government nature funding remains below international targets

Bezos Earth Fund has distributed $2.4 billion of its $10 billion pledge

Thousands of animal and plant species are at risk of disappearing, and conservation groups often need years of uninterrupted work to bring vulnerable populations back from the brink. Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sánchez Bezos are backing a new international effort that aims to give some of those projects more dependable financial support. As reported by Fortune, The Bezos Earth Fund has committed $100 million to the Species Recovery Alliance, a partnership involving 9 founding organisations and a combined $500 million commitment. Announced during a United Nations biodiversity summit in Armenia in October 2026, the initiative will support conservation programmes for species facing some of the highest risks of extinction.The Species Recovery Alliance was announced on 16 October at the Leaders’ Summit of COP17, the United Nations biodiversity conference held in Yerevan, Armenia. The Bezos Earth Fund is among 9 founding members, with its contribution accounting for $100 million of the initiative’s $500 million commitment, according to a spokesperson quoted by Fortune.The partnership brings together organisations with different conservation interests, including Re:wild, the environmental group co-founded by Leonardo DiCaprio, and Rainforest Trust.The other founding members are the Colossal Foundation, Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund, Fondation Segré, Franklinia Foundation, Ayers Wild Cat Conservation Trust and WildLives Earth.Rather than placing all the money in one shared pot, the members will manage their own grants while coordinating their work. Funding is intended for conservation organisations and local partners tackling threats to species classified by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) as endangered, critically endangered or extinct in the wild.Cristián Samper, managing director of the Bezos Earth Fund and its nature solutions lead, said a lack of dependable funding could put recovery efforts at risk even after conservation teams had made substantial progress.The IUCN Red List identifies more than 49,500 species as threatened with extinction. The new alliance will concentrate on three high-risk categories, which together cover more than 31,000 species.Its funding could support a range of interventions, depending on what each species needs. Some programmes may involve breeding animals in captivity before releasing them into the wild. Others may focus on rebuilding damaged habitats, reducing the spread of disease or controlling invasive species that threaten native wildlife.The alliance intends to track progress through the IUCN Red List and its Green Status of Species, which provides a way to assess conservation outcomes and the recovery of species over time.The new alliance follows another major commitment by the Bezos Earth Fund and Re:wild. In August 2026, the two organisations launched the Phoenix Species Project, pledging $100 million each towards a combined $200 million effort. That programme aims to recover 100 critically endangered species and species already extinct in the wild across 30 countries. Its targets include Madagascar’s golden-crowned sifaka, a rare lemur, and Australia’s elusive night parrot.The Phoenix initiative and the Species Recovery Alliance are separate efforts, although both involve the Bezos Earth Fund and an emphasis on reversing severe declines in wildlife populations.Lauren Sánchez Bezos, the fund’s vice chair, described the Phoenix project as a response to the possibility that children could grow up without ever encountering some of the animals that fascinate them. Her comments drew attention to a less visible aspect of extinction: species can disappear before future generations have a chance to know they existed.Private philanthropy is taking on a larger role as governments struggle to meet their biodiversity commitments. At the 2022 United Nations biodiversity summit in Montreal, countries agreed to mobilise $200 billion annually for biodiversity by 2030.Figures from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, cited by the Associated Press, put annual funding at between $75 billion and $92 billion from 2023 to 2025. That leaves a substantial gap between the money being raised and the level countries agreed to pursue. A United Nations progress report issued ahead of the October summit also found that fewer than half of national biodiversity targets were on track.Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the UN Convention on Biological Diversity, told the Associated Press that progress was not happening quickly enough. Alongside the private-sector alliance, 17 governments led by Colombia and Armenia launched a separate initiative known as the Coalition of Action to Recover Endangered Species, or CARES. The two efforts have different structures, but both seek to strengthen action on species facing extinction.Jeff Bezos established the Bezos Earth Fund in 2020 with a pledge of $10 billion to support climate action and nature conservation by 2030. The commitment was presented as the largest individual philanthropic pledge focused on climate and nature at the time.The fund has distributed $2.4 billion so far, a spokesperson told Fortune. More than $7 billion therefore remains to be allocated over the roughly four years leading up to the deadline. Fund officials told Bloomberg in May 2026 that they remained committed to the target.The latest species recovery commitment is part of a broader programme of grants. In recent months, the fund has announced $34 million for sustainable fabrics, $26 million for wildfire detection and $100 million for turning vacant urban land into parks in eight US cities. In September, it also announced more than $25 million in grants connected to the Pacific Ocean.
Article Summary: The Bezos Earth Fund has committed $100 million to the Species Recovery Alliance, a partnership involving 9 founding organisations and a combined $500 million commitment. The initiative will support conservation programmes for species facing some of the highest risks of extinction. The new alliance will concentrate on three high-risk categories, which together cover more than 31,000 species.

Article Title: Microsoft's ex-lawyer, and now Washington Governor, is angry with the company; says: I love the company, but 'what's up with ...'
Article Text:
Representative Image

What Microsoft ad says that made Governor 'upset'

What Washington Governor told Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce

Washington Governor Bob Ferguson is reportedly not happy with Microsoft. According to a report by GeekWire, Ferguson took aim at Microsoft over a political action committee's ad campaign criticizing the State government, speaking during what was intended to be an off-the-record business summit. Leaked audio obtained from the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce’s Regional Leadership Conference at the Suncadia resort shows Ferguson directly challenging the software giant. The audio was originally published by independent state politics newsletter The Washington Observer.At issue is an ad funded by Washington Needs to Compete, a PAC that state campaign finance records show has raised roughly $13.8 million -- including over $5 million directly from Microsoft, alongside contributions from CEO Satya Nadella, former CEO Steve Ballmer, and President Brad Smith. Other corporate donors include T-Mobile, F5, Alaska Airlines and Weyerhaeuser.The commercial reportedly targets the State capital, claiming that “Olympia is broken, spending more while you get less,” and features a line that particularly irked the governor: “In Washington, it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”As reported by GeekWire, Microsoft ad opens with a nod to “inventors in garages,” “mom-and-pop shops down Main Street” and farmers “feeding the world,” before declaring, “In Washington, it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”Then it turns, says: "But today, Olympia is broken, spending more while you get less." Jobs are leaving, the ad says, and “it’s harder than ever to afford a home and raise a family.” The ad, however, does not name Ferguson or any legislation. It ends by saying Olympia needs to "quit wasting money, fix what’s broken and put Washington families first."According to GeekWire, Ferguson repeated the words “it used to be” in disbelief before pressing the room of business and civic leaders. “What’s up with that?” Ferguson asked. “First, does anyone else in this room believe that? I sure as hell don’t.”Defending the state’s business climate, Ferguson cited PitchBook figures showing Seattle-area startups raised a record $3.5 billion in the third quarter—more than triple the amount from the same period a year earlier.The governor, a former Microsoft attorney who emphasized his respect for the company, voiced frustration that the spot aired during high-profile Seattle Seahawks broadcasts, reaching potential founders and transplants across the country. Records cited by GeekWire show the PAC spent $97,000 on an October 15 broadcast on Prime Video and $130,000 during an October 25 NBC telecast.“If we’re partners, partners should treat partners like partners, right?” Ferguson said, asking the audience to picture the backlash if he launched a multimillion-dollar campaign blasting Microsoft. “You guys would think I lost my mind if I did that.”While conceding that the State faces real hurdles, Ferguson urged the executives present to champion Washington’s strengths alongside its challenges, calling the region “so bloody special.” Ferguson, who assumed office in January 2025, also issued a firm reminder about his political horizon: “I plan on being governor for a long time,” he said, noting he intends to continue working with local business leaders, “Microsoft included. ”The Observer reported that Microsoft Olympia representative Michael Mattmiller was present and "kinda-sorta hugged it out afterward" with the governor. The report noted that Mattmiller declined to comment on the newsletter.
Article Summary: Washington Governor Bob Ferguson reportedly took aim at Microsoft over a political action committee's ad campaign criticizing the State government. Leaked audio obtained from the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce’s Regional Leadership Conference shows Ferguson directly challenging the software giant. At issue is an ad funded by Washington Needs to Compete, a PAC that state campaign finance records show has raised roughly $13.8 million.

Article Title: ChatGPT to teenagers: We will not answer your queries, how harmless they may be, if you ask about ...
Article Text:
Representative Image

What ChatGPT's change in policy means for kids

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you support stricter limits on weapons-related information provided to teens by AI chatbots? Yes, it's necessary for safety. No, it restricts access to information. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

OpenAI has announced that it is imposing stricter limits on the weapons-related information ChatGPT provides to teenage users, even when questions appear harmless. The changes form part of broader new safeguards designed to help prevent real-world violence. The company will restrict practical details about weapons and security systems that could be misused. These limits apply to users it predicts are under 18, regardless of whether the conversation shows any sign of violent intent.Existing rules already barred helping teens find or obtain weapons or assisting anyone in planning violence; the update extends those protections further. The move comes amid growing scrutiny of AI chatbots’ risks to young users and the industry’s responsibility in detecting potential threats of harm. OpenAI said that the new safeguards will begin rolling out in the coming weeks and will continue to be refined. Additional measures apply more broadly. For all users, ChatGPT will provide less detailed information about past mass attacks, including the weapons and equipment involved and how they were obtained. The chatbot will also be able to automatically end conversations in which a user appears fixated on violence, and the company may temporarily pause accounts after repeated such incidents.OpenAI has strengthened its age-prediction system to place estimated under-18 users into its dedicated teen experience and plans to notify parents if a teen’s account is paused for repeatedly discussing violence.The announcement accompanied a new Community Safety Report on the company’s violence-prevention efforts. OpenAI noted that it made more than 200 referrals to law enforcement in the third quarter of 2026 related to potential threats of violence. Teens will still be able to use ChatGPT for help preventing or de-escalating violence, seeking support, or connecting with a trusted adult.Here's what OpenAI's 'Community safety report and new protections for teens' say:"ChatGPT for Teens⁠ applies age-appropriate safeguards for users under 18, with stronger protections and additional limits to reduce exposure to sensitive content. We’re now placing further limits on weapons-related information teens can receive, even when a question appears harmless.Our policies already prohibit helping anyone plan or carry out violence and restrict helping teens find or obtain weapons. We’re extending those protections to restrict practical information about weapons and security systems that could be misused to facilitate violence, even when there’s no sign of violent intent. Teens can still use ChatGPT to help prevent and de-escalate violence, seek support, and connect with a trusted adult.We launched age prediction⁠ last year, which analyzes multiple signals such as behavior patterns to estimate whether a user may be under or over 18. We strengthened our age prediction system to continually assess new signals as people use ChatGPT and move teens into the under 18 experience when appropriate. Users who are incorrectly placed in the under 18 experience will always have a fast, privacy-protective way to confirm they are adults and have additional teen protections removed through Persona, our age verification partner.Our parental controls⁠ let parents link their ChatGPT accounts to their teens and manage safety settings together. Linked accounts include safety alerts⁠ that may be sent when specially trained reviewers identify a serious self-harm concern and behaviors that may be associated with disordered eating. In July, we expanded those alerts to notify parents if their teen’s account has been deactivated for violating our usage policies on violence. We are working to introduce notifications for parents if we pause their teen’s account for repeatedly discussing violence, as detailed above."
Article Summary: OpenAI has announced that it is imposing stricter limits on the weapons-related information ChatGPT provides to teenage users. The changes form part of broader new safeguards designed to help prevent real-world violence. These limits apply to users it predicts are under 18, regardless of whether the conversation shows any sign of violent intent.

Article Title: In August 2024, an island nation signed a treaty that will enable its citizens to live, work and study in Australia; now researchers wonder what happens to …
Article Text:
With a population of just about 9,500, Tuvalu is among the world’s most remote nations.

Why are Tuvaluans moving to Australia

What could happen to Tuvalu's traditional buildings

Poll Vote & Share your view How important is it to preserve traditional buildings in Tuvalu? Very important Somewhat important Not very important 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Can digital records help preserve Tuvalu's heritage

In August 2024, Tuvalu signed the Australia–Tuvalu Falepili Union treaty, giving its citizens a pathway to live, work and study in Australia. While the agreement creates new opportunities for people from the Pacific island nation, researchers are raising concerns about what could happen to its cultural heritage if more people move abroad. The concern is not just about losing homes and land to rising sea levels. Researchers say traditional buildings, construction skills and community spaces could also be lost as people move away and ways of life change.One example is the Lotolelei Church on Lakena, a small, uninhabited islet in Tuvalu. Although no one lives on the islet, families from neighbouring Nanumea still visit the church for religious services and family gatherings.Built in the early 20th century using timber brought from what is now Kiribati, the church remains an important link to the community's history.Tuvalu has a population of 9,646 and is investing in projects to protect its islands from rising sea levels. Its coastal adaptation and land-reclamation projects are expected to add around six hectares of land to the main island of Funafuti.At the same time, the Falepili Union treaty provides a pathway for Tuvaluans to move to Australia.Up to 280 permanent residency places are currently available each year through a ballot. These developments are giving people more options to remain in Tuvalu or move abroad. However, researchers say migration and climate adaptation plans also need to consider the country's cultural heritage.Researchers working with local communities have been documenting traditional buildings across Tuvalu through photographs, architectural drawings, interviews and 3D models.On the island of Niutao, the Makaili Hut is an example of how traditional buildings carry history across generations. Its earlier structure, known as Faleomanuka or the “house of wisdom”, was used as a communal storehouse and meeting place before its timber was reused to build a family home.Traditional construction methods, including carved wooden joints and coconut fibre lashings, remain visible in the structure. Researchers have also documented two classrooms in Funafuti that use building styles from different islands. Their designs reflect the identities and construction traditions of those communities.Researchers believe digital records could help preserve knowledge of traditional buildings and construction methods. They have created 3D models that Tuvaluans, including those living abroad, can explore through virtual reality.However, researchers say digital models cannot replace actual buildings or the knowledge passed down through generations. Community members have also suggested documenting traditional canoes, oral histories, gathering places and beaches.The researchers argue that decisions about migration, new land and existing settlements should include cultural heritage.
Article Summary: In August 2024, Tuvalu signed the Australia–Tuvalu Falepili Union treaty, giving its citizens a pathway to live, work and study in Australia. Researchers are raising concerns about what could happen to its cultural heritage if more people move abroad. The concern is not just about losing homes and land to rising sea levels, but traditional buildings, construction skills and community spaces.

Article Title: Billionaires are fighting a tax hike in California that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says he is good with as he is afraid of ...
Article Text:
“The fact that I can afford to pay $8 billion in taxes over five years is a privilege,”

“I’m not afraid of paying taxes.

I’m just afraid of being poor.”

What California’s Proposition 40 would do to billionaires

Billionaires spend millions fighting the measure

“I don’t mind paying taxes. The more you make, the more taxes you pay. I’m okay with that,” he said. “I am the ultimate American Dream.”

Why Huang says billionaires should remain in California

“I say to everybody, ‘Move to California, don’t leave.’ It’s the highest taxes in the world, but it’s okay,”

Jensen Huang isn’t against California’s proposed billionaire tax. While other wealthy tech executives are funding efforts to defeat Proposition 40 or have reduced their ties to the state, the Nvidia CEO said he doesn't mind paying more. The ballot measure would impose a one-time tax equal to 5% of the wealth of California residents worth more than $1 billion. If voters approve the measure on November 3, Huang could face an estimated $8 billion bill, paid over five years. However, he said he could afford it because of the opportunities he received in the US.he told CBS.Huang, who has spent decades living and building Nvidia in California, said education, access to talented people and the freedom to start a company helped make his career possible.Starting January 2026, Proposition 40 would apply to California residents with a net worth of more than $1 billion. It would impose a single charge on accumulated wealth, including investments and business holdings, rather than an annual income tax.The money would support state healthcare, public education, and food assistance programs. The tax could be paid in five yearly instalments. California’s official voter guide confirms that the measure would collect 5% of a qualifying resident’s wealth.Opponents argue that the measure could push wealthy residents out of California and reduce the income-tax revenue they would otherwise pay in future years. Supporters say billionaires can contribute more without substantially changing their standard of living.Technology billionaires and other wealthy donors have supplied more than $340 million to campaigns opposing Proposition 40 and related ballot measures. The opposition has reportedly spent more than $1 million a day.Google co-founder Sergey Brin has been a major contributor to the campaign, while former Google CEO Eric Schmidt and other Silicon Valley figures have also opposed the tax. Brin, Google co-founder Larry Page and former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick were among the wealthy executives who changed business or residential ties before the January cutoff.Huang has taken a different position.Huang has argued that California’s skilled workforce and culture of technology development outweigh its high taxes. Nvidia is headquartered in Santa Clara, near engineers, researchers, and other Silicon Valley companies.Huang said during an earlier appearance at Stanford Graduate School of Business.His acceptance of Proposition 40 does not mean he supports every proposed technology-related tax. Huang has questioned suggestions that companies should pay taxes on robots or AI tokens, arguing that governments could find other ways for productive businesses and individuals to contribute.
Article Summary: Jensen Huang says he can afford to pay $8 billion in taxes over five years. Proposition 40 would impose a one-time tax equal to 5% of the wealth of California residents worth more than $1 billion. Opponents argue that the measure could push wealthy residents out of California and reduce income-tax revenue they would otherwise pay.

Article Title: Knives Out director Rian Johnson made an iPhone camera app that shoots like his movies
Article Text:
Chromagraph Camera was originally made for Rian Johnson’s own use

Film director Rian Johnson , known for Knives Out, Glass Onion and Star Wars: The Last Jedi, has released an iPhone camera app that gives photos the same look as his movies. It's called Chromagraph Camera. It shoots in RAW and bypasses the iPhone's built-in image processing, using the colour science his cinematographer Steve Yedlin developed for their films instead.Chromagraph costs $12.99 (Rs 350 in India) as a one-time purchase, with no subscription or in-app purchases. Within a day of Johnson announcing it on X, it became the top paid app in the Photo & Video category on the US App Store, and his post has now crossed 11 million views.Johnson says he "badgered" Yedlin, who has shot all his films since Brick in 2005, into making his ideal iPhone camera. Yedlin built it with colour science programmer Eric Cameron. Johnson takes a lot of photos on his phone and simply wanted the app for himself, but Yedlin and Cameron decided to make it available to everyone.Chromagraph works a bit like a film camera. You frame and take the shot through the viewfinder, and the processed look only shows up when you open the gallery.Compared to the iPhone's default camera, photos come out darker and warmer, with grain and less digital sharpening. They also get halation, the soft glow that appears around bright lights on film. There are controls for colour, exposure, grain and halation, though they stay within Chromagraph's signature look.The original RAW files are kept in the gallery, so edits can be changed later. Photos can be exported as JPEG or HEIC, and an auto-export option sends every shot to the photo library.For now, Chromagraph only shoots stills. Johnson says video could come in the future, but likely only on the last few generations of Pro iPhones. There's no Android version either. He says Android hardware varies too much for a small team to tune the processing for every device. Chromagraph needs iOS 17 or later and already supports the iPhone Duo.
Article Summary: Chromagraph costs $12.99 (Rs 350 in India) as a one-time purchase, with no subscription or in-app purchases. Within a day of Johnson announcing it on X, it became the top paid app in the Photo & Video category on the US App Store.

Article Title: Google is changing the way developers optimise apps for foldables: What it means for users
Article Text:
Breaking the foldable stalemate

New tools to automate responsive design

Compose adaptive skill: Powered by AI coding agents, this tool audits compact mobile interfaces and scales them across foldables, tablets, Googlebooks, parked cars and XR headsets.

Desktop-ready controls: The tool automatically introduces critical desktop-grade inputs, such as custom pointer cursors, hover states, keyboard shortcuts and control tooltips.

Tabletop refactoring: For folding devices, the tool can automatically reorganise camera and media interfaces into dedicated tabletop modes when a device is partially bent.

Google announced at the Android Dev Summit that starting next year, the Google Play Store will actively evaluate how well apps and games perform on foldable screens. While the detailed criteria for the evaluation process will arrive later this year, the company has said that apps which adapt cleanly to these flexible displays will earn prime promotional placement and enhanced visibility across the store. The company has yet to clarify whether poorly adapted apps will suffer outright search penalties or simply forfeit featured discovery slots. As more people are likely to purchase foldable phones in the future, the apps’ user interface will be optimized for both cover and larger screens, giving users a better experience than before.Until now, Google has relied largely on voluntary design guidelines, as per a report by Android Authority For many developers, committing resources to rebuild apps for foldables was hard to justify given the category's smaller footprint compared to standard glass-slab phones. That adoption curve is shifting fast, the report said. With Apple’s entry via the iPhone Duo expanding the foldable audience, Google hopes broader hardware interest will encourage cross-platform optimisation.At the same time, the arrival of the Googlebook ecosystem adds fresh urgency. Running stretched, unoptimised phone layouts on larger laptop displays creates friction for users – a misstep Google admits even some of its own apps have made. By connecting Play Store discovery directly to foldable quality, Google aims to break through the chicken-and-egg dynamic that has kept development stalled.To help engineers modernise their software without maintaining separate codebases for every screen size, Google rolled out a suite of developer tool updates:

Article Title: How to stop WhatsApp from saving photos and videos to your phone’s gallery: A complete guide
Article Text:
Before you start: two different settings

On Android

Stop it for one chat or group only

On iPhone

Optional: Stop media from downloading automatically

You can still save the ones you want

Things to know

If your gallery is full of memes, forwarded good-morning images and photos from group chats you barely read, you’re not alone. WhatsApp automatically saves the photos and videos you receive to your phone’s gallery or camera roll, and you can turn this on or off at any time. Here is how to stop it on both Android and iPhone, for all chats or just a few.People often mix up two things, so it’s worth being clear. One setting controls whether WhatsApp shows downloaded media in your gallery. The other controls whether WhatsApp downloads media automatically over Wi-Fi or mobile data. WhatsApp regulates media auto-downloading independently of saving to your gallery. To clean up your gallery, you need the first one. To save mobile data and storage, you may want the second too.Stop all chats from appearing in your gallery•Open WhatsApp and tap the three-dot menu, then go to Settings.•Tap Chats.•Turn off Media visibility.This prevents newly downloaded media from showing up in your phone’s gallery, so photos and videos already there stay put and only new ones are affected.•Open the chat and tap the contact or group name at the top.•Tap Media visibility.•Select No in the pop-up window.This is useful for noisy family or college groups, while you keep saving photos from chats that matter.Stop all chats from saving to the camera roll•Open WhatsApp and tap Settings at the bottom right.•Open Chats and turn off Save to Camera Roll.With the setting off, incoming media stays inside WhatsApp until you save it yourself.Stop it for one chat only•Open the chat and tap the contact’s name or number at the top.•Under Save to Camera Roll, choose NeverIf you also want to save data and storage, you can stop WhatsApp from downloading media at all until you tap it.•Go to Settings > Storage and data (the menu names can vary slightly by version).•Under media auto-download, choose what happens on mobile data, Wi-Fi and roaming.•Set Photos, Audio, Video and Documents to Never if you want full control.Note that this changes how files are downloaded, not whether they appear in your gallery, so the two settings work best together.Turning these settings off doesn’t stop you from manually downloading the media you want to keep. Open the photo or video in the chat and use the save or download option to send it to your gallery whenever you choose.•Storage still gets used. Photos and videos you receive may still sit inside WhatsApp, so your phone’s memory isn’t freed unless you also clear chat media. Use Settings > Storage and data > Manage storage to review and delete large files.•Backups are separate. If iCloud Photos or Google Photos is on, anything in your gallery or camera roll can sync to the cloud, so turning off saving also reduces what gets uploaded.•Menus change. WhatsApp updates its settings often, and the wording may differ slightly on your phone, so look for the closest match if you can’t find an option.
Article Summary: WhatsApp automatically saves photos and videos you receive to your phone’s gallery or camera roll. To clean up your gallery, you need the first one. To save mobile data and storage, you may want the second too. Here is how to stop it on both Android and iPhone, for all chats or just a few.

Article Title: Meta, TikTok and X challenged a UK regulator's demand for detailed data on harmful posts and content removal, calling it excessively burdensome; an October 30 High Court ruling has rejected their case
Article Text:
Meta, TikTok and X lose UK court fight over Ofcom's content moderation data demands (Representational image; Reuters)

Ofcom's data demands cover removed posts and harmful content exposure

Court says the platforms never proved the burden was too heavy

Meta, TikTok and X have lost their legal fight against UK regulator Ofcom over how much data they must hand over under the Online Safety Act. On October 30, a Divisional Court at London's High Court dismissed their challenge to information notices Ofcom issued earlier this year, ruling the demands lawful and refusing to quash them.This was the first judicial review to test Ofcom's information powers under the 2023 Act, which sets tougher rules for social media platforms to protect children from harmful and illegal content. Lord Justice Singh and Mrs Justice Collins Rice threw out four of the five grounds as unarguable. The fifth, on proportionality, was allowed to proceed and then rejected too.The notices, sent in February under section 100 of the Act, sought detailed content moderation metrics. These included how many posts were removed or had their visibility restricted, and how many users were exposed to harmful content. WhatsApp received one too.The platforms called the demands unprecedented and said the data would cost millions of pounds to collect. TikTok said its notice required vast quantitative data spanning three years. X said it would have to run complex analysis on huge datasets it has no use for in its own business, a job that could take months.They also argued that Ofcom had sidestepped the Act's separate transparency regime and failed to carry out an impact assessment. TikTok alone claimed the decision had been made in advance.The judges disagreed on every count. The transparency regime is about publishing information, they said, while these notices serve Ofcom's own regulatory work. The law's wording is also broad enough that Ofcom didn't need a specific task in mind before asking.On proportionality, the court found the companies' evidence too thin to tip the balance. Their claim of an "extraordinary" burden had also never been put before Ofcom when it issued the notices.The ruling strengthens Ofcom's hand as it enforces a regime backed by fines of up to 10% of global turnover. Meta still has a separate challenge pending over how Ofcom calculates fees and potential fines. Until that lands, the three platforms have to start pulling together the numbers Ofcom asked for.
Article Summary: Court says the platforms never proved the burden was too heavy. Ruling strengthens Ofcom's hand as it enforces a regime backed by fines of up to 10% of global turnover. Meta still has a separate challenge pending over how Ofcom calculates fees and potential fines.

Article Title: Jeff Bezos's Earth Fund and three conservation partners have pledged an initial $12.5 million to support a Guyana forest-protection plan covering more than 2.4 million acres
Article Text:
In pic: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos

What the funding will support

“For Guyana, forest stewardship is not a sacrifice we make for development; it is the foundation of the development model we are building,”

Indigenous communities will have a role in planning

“This pledge backs Guyana’s conservation ambitions and the Indigenous stewardship that has helped keep these forests standing,”

More investment needed for Guyana’s 2030 goal

Jeff Bezos’s Earth Fund is backing forest protection in Guyana. The fund, Andes Amazon Fund, Nia Tero and Rainforest Trust announced a collective initial pledge of $12.5 million to support the country’s conservation plans, including proposed permanent protection for the Acarai–Rupununi Corridor. The corridor covers more than 1 million hectares, or approximately 2.4 million acres.According to the joint announcement, funding will support securing legal protection, establishing boundaries, and safeguarding the landscape against mining, industrial logging, and other incompatible activities. The pledge combines new and existing funding and supports Guyana’s wider ambition to protect 30% of its lands and waters by 2030. The government is advancing a proposal to permanently protect the corridor.The commitment follows President Irfaan Ali’s announcement that Guyana would advance the process of permanently protecting the corridor. The donors say their funding will support forest, freshwater, and biodiversity conservation while helping establish lasting legal safeguards. Conservation organisations and other eligible partners will implement it, working with the government, Indigenous Peoples, and local communities.The announcement does not break down how much each donor is contributing.Ali said.The partners said supported projects would uphold Indigenous rights, including Free, Prior and Informed Consent. That principle requires communities to make an informed choice about proposed activities affecting them before they proceed.Indigenous Peoples and local communities are also expected to participate in conservation planning, governance and management. The initiative aims to support their livelihoods while protecting the environment. Padu Franco, senior programme manager for the Andes and Amazon at the Bezos Earth Fund, linked the pledge to the fund’s broader rainforest work.he said.The Acarai–Rupununi Corridor forms part of Guyana’s broader conservation target, commonly described as “30×30”: protecting 30% of lands and waters by 2030.The donors said reaching that goal would require substantially greater, sustained investment from philanthropic, public and private sources. They described the initial pledge as a foundation for further work, including exploring long-term financing arrangements, strengthening conservation institutions and supporting community stewardship. The partners have invited additional public and private funders to contribute as Guyana develops the protection plan.
Article Summary: Jeff Bezos’s Earth Fund is backing forest protection in Guyana. The fund, Andes Amazon Fund, Nia Tero and Rainforest Trust announced a collective initial pledge of $12.5 million. The pledge supports Guyana's wider ambition to protect 30% of its lands and waters by 2030.

Article Title: Bernie Sanders warns Oracle, Nvidia and other technology companies on expenditure that has wiped billions from their market value; says: Don’t come begging to taxpayers, you ...
Article Text:
Bernie Sanders targets Musk over $366 million push to keep Republicans in power

Senator Bernie Sanders has a warning for technology companies on their ballooning AI expenditure. In the last few quarters, Silicon Valley's biggest technology companies -- Microsoft, Meta, Google, Amazon, SpaceX, Oracle and Nvidia -- have increased their capital expenditure by billions. Wall Street has not taken this kindly, so much so that it has wiped out billions from their stock value. According to a report in Reuters, "More than $2 trillion in market value is set to be wiped from the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 this month, as Big Tech earnings intensified investor scrutiny of whether the billions being poured ​into artificial intelligence can generate returns quickly enough."Hitting at rising AI debt, Senator Bernie Sanders slammed technology companies for what he called their risky AI bets. In a post on X, formerly Twitter, he told these companies not to come to taxpayers if their bet fails to deliver. "Companies like Microsoft, Meta, Google, Amazon, SpaceX, Oracle & Nvidia have racked up $3 trillion in debt on a high-stakes gamble on AI. Big Tech Oligarchs: If your AI bet fails, don’t come begging to taxpayers. You won’t be bailed out — period. End of Discussion," wrote Sanders.More than $2 trillion in market value is on track to be erased from the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 this month as Big Tech earnings intensify investor questions over whether the enormous sums being poured into artificial intelligence will deliver returns quickly enough.The Nasdaq 100 has already fallen more than 5.8% so far in October as the AI trade has hit turbulence. Hyperscalers including Meta Platforms, Alphabet and Amazon.com have raised their spending forecasts further while racing to expand AI infrastructure.$2 trillion-plus wiped out from Nasdaq 100Hyperscalers Meta, Google-parent Alphabet, and Amazon have all raised their forward-looking spending projections in recent months, committing hundreds of billions to compute clusters, custom chips, and data center infrastructure. However, with benchmark interest rates remaining elevated, Wall Street is growing increasingly uneasy about the rising cost of servicing capital investments that may take years to deliver meaningful profit margins.The reckoning was felt sharply on Thursday, when Alphabet suffered its largest single-day percentage decline on record. Investors reacted to slowing growth in the company's core search advertising unit alongside a steep rise in cash burn. Concurrently, Meta rattled markets with plans for a record $97.5 billion capital raise, sparking fears of equity dilution and raising concerns that tech giants may soon lean heavily on external financing to fund the AI arms race.AI companies’ growing reliance on debt funding is emerging as a fresh risk for investors, challenging the long-held view that the firms at the center of the boom are insulated from broader macroeconomic pressures. The concern is spreading beyond equities into credit markets, where investors are starting to price in the possibility that higher financing costs, combined with slower returns on AI spending, could squeeze companies previously regarded as relatively protected.Microsoft and SpaceX offered some relief from the gloom, delivering results that suggested AI spending is beginning to pay off. Microsoft posted quarterly results that suggested commercial AI applications are beginning to translate into revenue gains, offering a rare bright spot amid the tech sector selloff."It may be that we've overestimated how strong the growth might be, but they're not going negative in aggregate," John Bilton, global head of strategic research for multi-asset solutions at JPMorgan Asset Management, told Reuters. "We have an insatiable and growing demand for data," he added.Market focus now turns to next week, when Apple is scheduled to report its quarterly earnings, followed by Nvidia in mid-November. Nvidia's forward guidance, in particular, is viewed by analysts as the definitive litmus test for whether hardware demand can withstand cooling sentiment across the broader tech landscape.
Article Summary: $2 trillion in market value is set to be wiped from the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 this month. Wall Street is growing increasingly uneasy about the rising cost of servicing capital investments that may take years to deliver meaningful profit margins. Microsoft and SpaceX offered some relief from the gloom, delivering results that suggested AI spending is beginning to pay off.

Article Title: LinkedIn cofounder Reid Hoffman defends AI datacenters; his advice to tech companies ‘make sure the…’
Article Text:
Reid Hoffman

Escalating debate over infrastructure costs

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you believe should be prioritized by tech companies when constructing AI data centers? Community Benefits Environmental Impact Local Job Creation 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

As the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) data centres faces growing scrutiny across America, LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman is pushing back against critics, arguing that the massive wave of datacenter construction is keeping the US economy afloat. He said that it is the responsibility of the tech companies building the infrastructure to ensure there are no problems faced by nearby residents. Speaking on the Newcomer podcast recently, he gave advice to tech giants to address mounting neighbourhood pushback directly while pointing to the immediate macroeconomic boost.“Make sure the local community gets a sustainable benefit. Make sure noise, the environment, and everything else is taken care of. Make sure electricity prices stay the same or go down. And then allow the local community to say, ‘I want it, I don’t want it,’ and exercise their right to self-determination," he said, outlining clear conditions that developers must satisfy before moving forward with new builds.The rush to construct facilities capable of training and running advanced AI models has ignited both political and social resistance across the US due to increased strain on power grids and drinking water supply.Data centres require tremendous amounts of power to run and cool high-density servers, sparking fears of strained regional power grids and higher residential utility bills. Similarly, heavy cooling requirements have raised persistent worries over the strain placed on local water supplies, alongside concerns over persistent facility noise.While the initial building phase drives demand for skilled trades like electricians and carpenters, completed datacenters require relatively few permanent operational workers on-site. Hoffman, however, defended the record capital flowing into AI facilities, claiming the investments deliver wide-reaching economic benefits far beyond Silicon Valley balance sheets.“All of this capital infusion, people think, ‘Oh, that’s just going to tech companies’ (...) but a massive percentage of it is going toward data center construction, which means construction electricians, carpenters, real estate development, and so on (...) and because of that, that capital is the only reason we’re not in a recession,” Hoffman said.Some tech giants announced their quarterly earnings, suggesting that there is no slowdown in capital expenditure when it comes to infrastructure spending. Google-parent Alphabet lost $500 billion in market value post announcements after it held its guidance at $195 billion to $205 billion.
Article Summary: LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman says datacenter construction is keeping the US economy afloat. He says tech companies must ensure there are no problems faced by nearby residents. The rush to construct facilities capable of training and running advanced AI models has ignited both political and social resistance.

Article Title: Reed Jobs, who lost his father Steve Jobs to cancer, has taken how to fight the disease as his life's work, now he sees a common anti-obesity drug bringing a revolution
Article Text:
Reed Jobs, who lost his father Steve Jobs to cancer, has taken how to fight the disease as his life's work, now he sees a common anti-obesity drug bringing a revolution

A personal mission born from his father's diagnosis

Why Reed Jobs is betting on GLP-1 drugs

Comparing obesity to smoking

Research suggests potential Cancer benefits

A different vision of victory against cancer

Reed Jobs, the son of Apple founder Steve Jobs , has made the fight against cancer a central mission of his life after losing his father to pancreatic cancer. That path led him to start Yosemite, an oncology-focused venture capital firm. Now, the founder of an oncology-focused venture capital firm, he believes that a class of anti-obesity drugs known as GLP-1s could play a major role in preventing cancer and other chronic diseases. According to a Fortune report, Jobs described the medicines as some of "the most impactful drugs that we've ever made." Jobs says the firm’s second fund has passed its $350 million target.After Steve Jobs was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in 2003, Reed Jobs started working in cancer research laboratories and later studied pre-med at Stanford University, determined to help find better ways to combat the disease. This journey eventually led Jobs to start Yosemite, which is an investment focused firm which exclusively works on oncology. Speaking to Fortune's Term Sheet, Jobs mentioned that the company’s second funding round has already exceeded its target $350 million, reflecting growing investor interest in cancer-related innovation.In a recent Term Sheet interview with Fortune’s Allie Garfinkle, Jobs said he is excited about experimental cancer vaccines, but also about GLP-1 drugs, the class of medicines widely used for weight loss.He calls them among the most impactful drugs ever made. In his view, they will help people who are obese and struggling with it, and will also affect cancer, cardiovascular disease and many other conditions.His argument is that GLP-1s could help prevent cancer by cutting obesity, which the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) links to a higher risk of 13 types of cancer. The CDC estimates that obesity-associated cancers make up 40 percent of all cancers diagnosed in the US each year, including colon, pancreatic, kidney and breast cancer.Jobs compared obesity to smoking, saying the longer someone lives with either risk factor, the greater their chances of developing certain cancers. A 2024 study cited by Fortune found that smoking caused an estimated 19.3 percent of US cancer cases, compared with 7.6 percent linked to excess body weight. He said GLP-1s are a fantastic way for obese people to stop being obese very quickly.“The more time you spend being obese, the greater your odds of getting an obesity-related disease are,” he said. “[GLP-1s] are a fantastic way for obese people to basically stop being obese very quickly.”Some scientific studies have begun to explore whether the benefits of GLP-1 drugs extend beyond weight loss. Jobs pointed to growing evidence that reducing obesity may also lower cancer risk. A study published in JAMA Oncology in 2025 followed more than 86,000 adults eligible for anti-obesity medications and found that patients taking GLP-1 drugs had a 17% lower risk of developing the cancers examined in the study compared with non-users. Jobs acknowledged that the medications are not without drawbacks, including concerns about muscle loss, but argued that their emergence represents one of biotechnology's biggest breakthroughs in recent years.Despite advancement in the cancer research, Jobs revealed that he does not believe that humanity will ever be able to eliminate the disease completely. This is because the human cells can always mutate and become cancerous, and he feels that total eradication is an unrealistic goal. However, he hopes that cancer can eventually be managed in a similar way as HIV, where the patients can live a long and healthy life with the help of ongoing treatment. “It’s the victory over death, and that is what I want for cancer patients, and I think that that’s more achievable and more realistic,” Jobs said.
Article Summary: Reed Jobs, the son of Apple founder Steve Jobs, has made the fight against cancer a central mission of his life after losing his father to pancreatic cancer. Now, the founder of an oncology-focused venture capital firm, he believes a class of anti-obesity drugs known as GLP-1s could play a major role in preventing cancer.
